prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the analysis of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: tractable time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts and interest-rate rules, and a microfounded, welfare-based framework for evaluating policy

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B001 as a single part, credited to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. What changed is how I justify the attribution, which the chair's questions pressed on. The criterion I apply is origin of the separable ideas that the field's later work takes as given. Calvo supplied the tractable time-dependent pricing device that makes an aggregate supply block usable. Taylor supplied the staggered-contract model and the interest-rate rule as a positive and normative benchmark for policy. Woodford integrated these into a welfare-based, microfounded framework for evaluating policy. Identified estimation (Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans), the empirical canon (Galí, Gertler, Clarida) and central-bank adoption (Smets) are important, but they build on that structure. They would support a different citation, one about quantification and use, and a different laureate set. I would not choose between the two criteria by weighing practical influence alone. I think the originating-ideas criterion is the more defensible reading of a discovery prize, and it avoids the Gertler overlap with B002 and the 2022 prize. On the Taylor rule, I rest Taylor's credit mainly on staggered contracts and on the rule's role as an analytical benchmark that was later tested and extended. I would not credit it as a policy prescription. The core ideas are roughly 25 to 45 years old. The 2008 crisis, the zero lower bound and the post-2021 inflation have produced extensions (state dependence, heterogeneous agents, financial frictions) that use this framework as their reference point. I read those episodes as limits on the descendants and on the literal Calvo description, not as a refutation of a prize centred on the originating ideas. I accept that this is a judgement, and the case does not rest on how many colleagues prefer it. My assessment relies on general knowledge and the supplied files, not on independent verification.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the strongest objection. Any trio leaves out contributors with real claims: Galí and Gertler on the canonical model and its empirical use, Christiano and Eichenbaum on identified estimation, and Smets on adoption. Priority questions around Fischer and Phelps also remain, and Clarida is not on the ballot. The originating-ideas criterion is a choice. A committee that valued making the framework quantitatively usable would reach a different set. Members who prefer B006 argue that its three-name attribution is cleaner than this one, and I think that argument has real weight. The empirical record is also mixed: the Phillips-curve fit, evidence of state-dependent pricing in micro data, and the 2021-23 inflation. If the committee cannot settle attribution, B006 with Persson, Tabellini and Besley is the better-bounded candidate. It would also be wrong to treat the convergence of proposals on the same three names as evidence of merit. Convergence suggests the originators are widely identified, nothing more.

responses.point: Dreber moved B001 up to her first alternative after reading Krusell's separability argument. She still treats the post-2021 Phillips-curve evidence as unresolved and doubts that B002 can reach six votes.
responses.response: I agree that the empirical question is unresolved and I do not claim the framework came through intact. My reply is that the unresolved part concerns the quantitative descendants and the literal Calvo description, not the contribution being rewarded. I do accept your point that the post-2021 evidence limits how strongly a citation can speak about the framework's success, so my citation says 'analysis of' and 'framework for evaluating policy' and makes no claim about forecasting performance. I also agree that shared rankings are not merit, and that applies to my own B001 ranking. On B002, I accept that Kiyotaki-Moore is the cleaner attribution, and I keep it below B001 because of the 2022 overlap and the Gertler complication.

responses.point: Strömberg moved from B015 to B001. He argues the award rests on the originating ideas (pricing device, contract structure, policy-rule framework), not on DSGE forecasting, and says B006's trio is arguably cleaner than B001's.
responses.response: I agree with the originating-ideas framing, and it is the criterion I now state explicitly. It separates the three proposed names from the estimation-side claimants, and I would keep that distinction in the citation. I also agree with you on B006 attribution being cleaner, and I count it against B001. It does not change my ranking, because the difference in how widely the framework is used in policy analysis still seems larger to me than the difference in attribution clarity. I take your point that B015 has a clear paper-level attribution but narrow shared support. That is a reason to leave it off my alternatives list, not a view on its science.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B006 first and argues that B001's caveats (a trio that could shift toward Galí or Gertler, the Gertler overlap, the post-2008 and post-2021 debates) are attribution or durability concerns that B006 mostly lacks. She also proposes wording the B006 citation around the framework, not around settled causal effects.
responses.response: I agree with your diagnosis of my own caveats, and the disagreement between us is mainly about how to weigh them. I give more weight to breadth of influence and to the absence of a recent neighbouring prize, and you give more weight to clean credit. B006's 2024 neighbour is a real consideration for me, and so is the weaker cross-country identification, although you are right that the framework-first wording answers part of it. I am not fully persuaded on the Besley question. I would accept your three-name version if B006 advances, since a distinct state-capacity strand is a coherent reading. I would also accept Persson and Tabellini alone, as Hassler proposes. Please note that I disclose a Lund colleague relationship with you below.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, ranks B002 first and B001 as an alternative. He treats B001's crowded credit as a larger attribution cost than anything in B002, and he says its attribution is a hard problem he has not resolved.
responses.response: I agree it is hard, and I do not claim the criterion makes it easy. The disagreement is on how much a harder attribution should cost. I would pay it for a body of work with a larger documented effect on how policy is analysed. I also take your answer to my 2022 overlap point. Bank runs and the Great Depression differ from collateral-driven amplification in production economies, so I now regard the overlap as a smaller concern than in round 1. The remaining reason I keep B002 below B001 is that the financial-accelerator strand (Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist) and Kiyotaki-Moore are parallel lines. That makes the unclaimed credit less clear than you describe, and your calibrated-versus-identified caveat applies. I cannot name later empirical work that settles it, and I have not verified any.

responses.point: Boppart now calls Calvo-Taylor-Woodford the more defensible trio, while he keeps B021 (Helpman, Melitz) as his preferred part because its two-person attribution is cleaner. He lists B001 as an alternative.
responses.response: Thank you for revising your opening, which used Galí in place of Calvo. That removes the main dispute on B001's laureate set. I agree that Helpman-Melitz is a cleaner two-name case, and I keep B021 as my second alternative. I treat Redding as a successor on the quantitative and spatial extensions. I share the concern about Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, since a citation about the exporter facts would be incomplete. A citation about the selection model and gains from trade could stand. If B021 advanced, I would want that wording. On Krugman 2008, I find your argument for a distinct unit of analysis (the firm, not the industry) persuasive, although I do not treat it as settled.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept origin of ideas as the criterion that separates Calvo, Taylor and Woodford from Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, or will prefer one that rewards quantification and adoption. The latter would change the laureate set, and any Gertler credit would also overlap with B002 and the 2022 prize.

How the committee treats Taylor's credit, as a scientific contribution through staggered contracts and the rule as a benchmark, or as a policy prescription, and how it resolves priority questions involving Calvo, Taylor, Fischer and Phelps.
How much weight the post-2021 inflation episode, the micro evidence on state-dependent pricing and the heterogeneous-agent critique should carry against a prize centred on the originating ideas.
Whether the cleaner attribution of B006 should outweigh B001's breadth of influence, and whether B006 should be framed as Persson and Tabellini only or with Besley.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied files. I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or the strength of later empirical work.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Calvo, Taylor or Woodford is apparent from my supplied profile, and my market-design field is not close to B001. I disclose, without adjudicating: Kerstin Enflo (B006 preferred) is a Lund colleague, as she notes in her own file, and Jan Teorell (B006 preferred) was formerly at Lund; neither relationship concerns the candidate work. I am also an SSE affiliate alongside committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg, and I co-authored COVID policy work with SSE economists (Östling, Lindqvist). None of these ties involves a credited candidate. I gave the 2020 presentation speech on behalf of the Academy. That speech may reflect collective drafting and does not establish a private preference here. I have no documented tie to the B006 or B021 credited names, which are my alternatives.
